me_1_lower_pond_crag.blurb: Lower Pond Crag is a band of gneiss cliff above Lower Pond, one of the Chain of Ponds crags in western Maine, roughly half an hour northwest of Sugarloaf. Around twenty single-pitch lines are on offer, about two-thirds trad and the rest bolted. The difficulty is lopsided: a few easy lines in the 5.7 to 5.8 range, a small handful of 5.10s, and the biggest group sitting at 5.11, so it suits leaders who are comfortable on harder pitches. A talus field lies between the road and the base. Many of the lines carry good ratings from visitors, and a rocky swimming beach sits beside the pullout.
me_1_lower_pond_crag.parking_note: Use the roadside pullout on Route 27 by the utility pole, about 0.6 miles beyond the Gold Brook DOT lot when coming from the Eustis and Stratton side. A rocky swimming beach is right beside it.

md_balcony_jr.blurb: Balcony Jr. is a short wall running along a power line clearing above the river at Harpers Ferry, next door to the larger Balcony Rock. Close to thirty lines are packed in: mostly trad leads, a few top-rope laps, about ten boulder problems and a single bolted line. Roped climbs run from around 5.6 up to 5.11, with the 5.10 range the busiest. Boulder problems start at V0 and top out near V5, with most at the easy end. The walk in is a steady uphill of roughly a quarter hour, which is a fair price for a mixed crag where a party with varied abilities can all find something.

md_middle_earth.blurb: Middle Earth is a wooded cliff on Sugarloaf Mountain in central Maryland and one of the two busiest crags on the mountain. The broken wall stretches about 120 feet, with most lines 30 to 40 feet tall and a few longer. Trees surround it, so it stays shaded even on a hot day. Climbing is mostly trad, with some top-rope laps, and Sugarloaf has no bolts. Grades span from easy fifth-class up to 5.12, though the bulk sit between 5.5 and 5.10, making it a good pick for newer leaders and mixed groups. Expect company on weekends, including hikers who may wander along the clifftop.
md_middle_earth.parking_note: Leave the car in the West View lot on Sugarloaf Mountain. The green-blazed trail to the crag begins beside the toilets and shack near the lot entrance.

md_right_fork_rocks.blurb: Right Fork Rocks is a small, out-of-the-way outcrop inside the Frederick Watershed north of Frederick, Maryland, split into four little sections. It is mainly a top-rope spot: over twenty lines set up from above, only a couple of leads, and one aid line. Grades begin in the beginner range and climb to 5.10, where the largest cluster sits, and ratings may run stiff for their numbers. The base is level and roomy, so spreading out gear is easy. Expect some litter and fire rings around the rocks, so bring a bag and pack out more than you brought.
md_right_fork_rocks.parking_note: From Frederick, head north on US 15 about nine miles, take the Hansonville Road exit, then Mountaindale Road to a T and turn left. When the pavement ends, stay right at the fork on the rough dirt road and drive about a mile to a tiny pullout just before a sharp left bend. The rock is about 100 feet away across the stream.

md_north_bank_tulip_area.blurb: The Tulip Area is the first boulder cluster you meet on the trail at Northwest Branch, a wooded creek corridor just north of Washington DC. About two dozen problems are gathered around two main boulders, and the range is friendly: most are V0 to V2, with a sprinkling of V3 to V5 and one standout at V7. Lots of easy warm-ups make it a good first stop for beginners, and the quick walk from the lot means it sees plenty of traffic. Some problems sit close to the water, so watch the landings when the creek runs high.
md_north_bank_tulip_area.approach: Follow the trail from the parking lot, passing a lone boulder at the water's edge. The Tulip Area is the first big group of boulders on your right, within about a minute.

md_2_ed_rocks.blurb: 2 Ed Rocks is the biggest wall on the main outcrop of the Thurmont Watershed near Thurmont, Maryland, standing at the far right end on an open, sunny hillside and rising close to 42 feet. Most of the lines are top-ropes, with a handful of trad leads and a few that suit beginners. Grades run from 5.4 to 5.11, with the heart of the wall between 5.6 and 5.10, and a good cluster of low 5.6 to 5.7 lines for easing in. The walk-in is a stiff uphill, so it works best for a group that wants a full day on ropes.
md_2_ed_rocks.parking_note: Pull off along Pryor Road, about a fifth of a mile north of where it meets US 15. There is only room for two or three cars.
md_2_ed_rocks.approach: Walk uphill on the fire road for roughly twenty minutes, then branch onto the trail on the east side, which leads straight to the rock.
